articles.title: NTSB details warning whistles and emergency orders before tanker collision capsized New Orleans riverboat
articles.summary: NTSB investigators detail warning whistles and emergency orders captured on the tanker's voyage recorder before the New Orleans riverboat collision.
articles.body: A tanker suffered a steering problem about two minutes before slamming into a docked New Orleans riverboat Friday, federal investigators said Sunday, detailing warning whistles, calls for help and emergency orders before the collision. The Atlantic Asphalt was heading upriver near the Crescent City Connection Bridge at about 12:26 p.m. when its rudder remained turned to the right, sending the ship toward the Mississippi River’s east bank, National Transportation Safety Board senior marine accident investigator Bart Barnum said. The tanker struck American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage at about 12:28 p.m. The riverboat capsized in about 22 minutes, according to preliminary information presented by the NTSB. NEW ORLEANS BOAT CRASH CALLED ‘MIRACLE ON THE MISSISSIPPI’ AS EVERYONE IS ACCOUNTED FOR, OFFICIALS SAY Investigators downloaded more than nine hours of data from the tanker’s voyage data recorder, including bridge audio, rudder angle, engine RPM, course and speed. The recordings captured sounds consistent with the ship’s whistle, warnings and requests for assistance over its marine radio, commands to deploy anchors and emergency shiphandling orders, Barnum said. 11-NIGHT CARIBBEAN CRUISE ABRUPTLY CANCELED AFTER COAST GUARD DETAINS SHIP Officials described the steering problem as a "steering casualty," but cautioned that the term does not establish what went wrong. "It could be many different things. That is something that we are investigating very closely," Barnum said. AT LEAST 6 PEOPLE INJURED AFTER BOSTON DUCK BOAT OVERTURNS NEAR ENTRANCE TO POPULAR TOURIST ATTRACTION NTSB board member John DeLeeuw said investigators have data on the tanker’s speed but are still analyzing it before releasing it publicly. Video showed anchors were down, but investigators are still determining which ones were deployed and how far, he said. The findings follow a frantic rescue effort that officials said left everyone aboard the American Heritage alive. Roughly 100 people were pulled from the Mississippi River, while responders evacuated more than 80 before the vessel overturned, Port of New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said Saturday. TWO DEAD, INCLUDING INFANT, AFTER BOAT CAPSIZES IN NEW YORK HARBOR; 12 RESCUED "This is a miracle. It is a literal miracle on the Mississippi," Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry said Friday. Eight people remained hospitalized Saturday, including two in serious condition. The other six were stable, officials said. FBI INVESTIGATES SUSPECTED HOMICIDE ABOARD MSC SEASCAPE CRUISE SHIP AFTER SUDDEN RETURN TO TEXAS The NTSB said Sunday that 140 passengers and 50 crew members were aboard the riverboat, a total of 190. New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno also said the American Heritage’s captain was injured but stayed aboard until passengers and crew were accounted for, becoming the last person to leave. MOM LOSES GRIP ON DAUGHTER AS PASSENGER FERRY CAPSIZES WITH 20 PEOPLE STILL MISSING "Every moment of the critical time [Friday], he did not want to leave his ship," Moreno said Saturday. Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said Saturday that crews were preparing to remove 16,000 gallons of fuel before salvage operations, warning that removing the capsized vessel could take weeks. DeLeeuw said Sunday that divers had been in the water, with salvage work overseen by the Coast Guard and salvage companies. UNLICENSED NYC BOAT OPERATOR ALLEGEDLY IGNORED SAFETY WARNINGS BEFORE MOTHER, BABY DIED IN CAPSIZING: FEDS Interviews with American Heritage crew members were underway Sunday. Interviews with the Atlantic Asphalt’s crew were scheduled to begin Monday and continue through the week, Barnum said. Sunday’s briefing was its last planned on-site news conference, DeLeeuw said, with further updates to be posted online. Fox News Digital's Brittany Miller contributed to this report.

articles.title: Notorious Mexican drug lord, who was convicted of killing US DEA agent, dies at 80
articles.summary: Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, founder of one of Mexico’s first major drug cartels whose conviction for the 1985 killing of a US drug-enforcement agent made him one of the country’s most notorious traffickers, died in hospital on Sunday at age 80.
articles.body: Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, founder of one of Mexico’s first major drug cartels whose conviction for the 1985 killing of a US drug-enforcement agent made him one of the country’s most notorious traffickers, died in hospital on Sunday at age 80. Local security authorities said Félix Gallardo was transferred to a private hospital in the western city of Guadalajara two days ago but suffered multiple organ failure and died around 2 p.m. on Sunday. Imprisoned since 1989, Félix Gallardo was an inmate in a maximum-security prison in western Jalisco state, though his lawyers repeatedly sought house arrest on the grounds of his deteriorating health. Rising to prominence in the 1970s, the former cartel kingpin was an architect of Mexico’s modern drug-trafficking trade, igniting a series of turf wars that have led to hundreds of thousands of deaths and disappearances in ensuing decades. His rise and fall was portrayed on screen by Mexican actor Diego Luna in the 2018 hit Netflix series “Narcos: Mexico.” Born in 1946 in Culiacan, Sinaloa, a northwestern state that would later become synonymous with narco-trafficking, he worked as a police officer and bodyguard for a local governor then became a powerful criminal capo known as the “boss of bosses.” Félix Gallardo and others set up the cartel in Guadalajara, the Jalisco state capital and a fast-growing economic powerhouse, becoming the first to move cocaine to the US on a massive scale and to forge an alliance with Colombian drug barons, including Pablo Escobar’s Medellin cartel. His narcotics empire expanded in the 1970s and 1980s thanks to bribes that won protection from corrupt officials and innovations like using light aircraft to move drugs across the continent, supported by fellow kingpins like Rafael Caro Quintero. His legal battles stretched across decades. Arrested in 1989, Félix Gallardo was sentenced to 40 years in prison on drug-trafficking and weapons charges tied to the Guadalajara cartel. While already incarcerated, he faced a separate prosecution over the 1985 kidnapping and murder of US Drug Enforcement Administration agent Enrique “Kiki” Camarena and Mexican pilot Alfredo Zavala Avelar. Camarena’s killing caused a diplomatic dispute with Washington, which pressed Mexico hard to arrest those involved. In 2017, a federal court found Félix Gallardo guilty in that case and imposed a further 37-year sentence. He denied responsibility for the killings. Félix Gallardo suffered poor health in his final years, and was blind in one eye, practically deaf and unable to walk on his own by the time Spanish-language US network Telemundo interviewed him in prison in 2021. He maintained his innocence. “Thirty-two years have passed… That’s an eternity for a man who did not commit any crime,” he said.

articles.title: TikToker arrested after big cat mauls teen to death during video shoot at private farm
articles.summary: A TikToker and farm owner were arrested after a big cat fatally mauled a teenage worker during a video shoot in Pakistan, Lahore officials said.
articles.body: A TikToker has been arrested alongside a farm owner after a big cat viciously mauled a teenage employee to death during a video shoot in eastern Pakistan, officials said Thursday. The attack happened at a private breeding farm near Kahna, according to The Times of India. The animal "got out of control in the presence of the TikToker, who had come to the farmhouse to make a TikTok video, leaving a farm employee critically injured," Lahore police said in a post on X. Although police described the animal as a lioness, a photo shared by the agency alongside its statement appeared to show a tiger. 'LOOKSMAXXING' INFLUENCER CLAVICULAR CHARGED AFTER ALLEGEDLY SHOOTING DEAD ALLIGATOR ON LIVESTREAM The victim, 19, was identified as Talha, while the arrested farm owner was identified as Fayyaz and the TikToker as Noman, according to The Times of India. The outlet added that the TikToker had reportedly asked for the animal to be released from its enclosure for a TikTok video shoot. After the attack, Talha was rushed to a private hospital but died while undergoing treatment. **GRAPHIC WARNING** NEARLY 100 MONKEYS ESCAPE ENCLOSURE, INVADE NEIGHBORHOODS AS OFFICIALS SCRAMBLE TO RECAPTURE THEM Police opened a case into the incident and uncovered an alleged attempt to "conceal the truth." "An attempt was made to pass off the lioness attack as a dog attack," police said. Investigators are examining whether the farm had the proper permits to keep the big cat, whether adequate safety measures were in place and whether negligence played a role in the attack. articles.title: China’s ‘miracle city’ that no US president has visited (yet)
articles.summary: China’s tech metropolis has more billionaires than any city outside New York. And next week it will get a visit from the world’s most famous billionaire New Yorker.
articles.body: China’s preeminent tech metropolis has more billionaires than any city outside New York. And this week it will get a visit from the world’s most famous billionaire New Yorker. Donald Trump will become the first sitting US president to land in Shenzhen when he arrives for an APEC summit where Chinese leader Xi Jinping will show off the urban microcosm of his nation’s modern story: high-level planning, roaring technological advancement, and rapid wealth creation. There, a stone’s throw from Hong Kong, Trump will find China’s answer to Silicon Valley; a futuristic city that’s home to tech entrepreneurs, food-delivering drones and the world’s fastest supercomputer. It’s a city that launched many of the tech advances that have put Trump and Xi on a collision course over access to raw materials, advanced chips, and lucrative markets. (A fragile trade truce between the world’s two biggest economies will expire in January.) And it’s quickly becoming one of China’s top destinations for foreign travelers. If you chat with any of Shenzhen’s 18 million people, they will proudly tell you it is a “miracle city.” Built out of mangrove wetlands over just four decades, the gleaming city boasts more skyscrapers than New York City and roughly three times more than Chicago, according to the Council on Vertical Urbanism. One of these megastructures resembles the tip of a bamboo shoot, while another looks like a folded sheet of metal. It also boasts the world’s fifth-tallest building: the Ping An Finance Centre. Walking through its streets, everything feels brand new. Self-driving electric taxis purr quietly along the roads, while drones fly around delivering hot meals and iced coffee. Crystal-like orbs dangle from roadside trees, collecting solar energy and illuminating the streets at night. The names of those streets are also telling: Talent Park; Start-up Road; Garden of Knowledge; and many named after famous Chinese scientists. In its myriad sleekly designed cafes, young people – the city’s average age is only 32 – earnestly talk about ways to make more cash, and polished middle-aged parents discuss where they should send their children to study abroad. Backwater to megacity Fifty years ago – around the time a bullish young Trump was inking his first Manhattan real-estate deal – this city did not exist. What stood there was an economic backwater surrounded by farmland where families struggled to put enough food on the table, overshadowed by a much wealthier city across the water, the British enclave of Hong Kong. A farmer who kept more than three ducks would be condemned as “pursuing a capitalist path,” according to a documentary on Shenzhen released in 2019 by state broadcaster CCTV. China’s then paramount leader Deng Xiaoping was desperate to liberalize the economy of his isolated and impoverished country, which was still recovering from the decade-long trauma of the Cultural Revolution. It was Xi’s father, Xi Zhongxun – then governor of Guangdong province, which includes Shenzhen – who suggested that Deng use several towns on China’s southern coast to stage experiments in free-market economics to attract foreign capital. Shenzhen was chosen for its proximity to Hong Kong, from which – it was hoped – it would learn about modern business practices. The government offered financial incentives for the best talents to head to the city. Among them were Chen Daiyao’s grandparents, who arrived in Shenzhen in 1983. Back then they thought Shenzhen “was pretty shabby,” the 33-year-old university assistant professor told CNN. But they would not be alone in heeding the call of this free-market incubator. Four years later, former People’s Liberation Army engineer Ren Zhengfei founded his own company in Shenzhen – taking advantage of a new law allowing researchers to establish their own firms for the first time. A decade later, Wang Chuanfu left his job at a battery maker to follow the same dream. The companies they founded in Shenzhen are now some of the best-known in the world – Ren’s Huawei is one of the world’s biggest tech conglomerates, while BYD, the company Wang founded, overtook Elon Musk’s Tesla to become the world’s biggest seller of electric vehicles last year. “At the time, Shenzhen offered what was probably the best environment in China for innovation and entrepreneurship,” Wang told CCTV in 2019. The two firms will be on display at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, where the “official designated vehicles” are advanced BYD models, powered in no small part by Huawei technologies. The city is also home to several other business behemoths driving China’s rapid transformation, including social media giant Tencent and DJI, the world’s largest drone maker. As a child, Chen could feel the speed of her hometown’s development. “By the time I was in primary school, the city was already urbanizing at a remarkable pace.” In 1990, the city became the first in China to have a McDonald’s restaurant – with the appearance of the American chain’s iconic golden arches viewed as a milestone moment in China’s opening up. The APEC invitations last year saluted the city’s remarkable journey. “Shenzhen has transformed from a backward little fishing village into a modern international metropolis over the past few decades,” hailing the achievement as – there’s that word again – “a miracle.” Development at the pace and scale of Shenzhen’s is much easier to accomplish in a top-down, one-party state, observers say. Draw for Western visitors Even before APEC hosting duties put it on the diplomatic map, Shenzhen had rapidly become foreign tourists’ second-favorite Chinese destination, behind only Shanghai. In 2025, more than 2 million foreign tourists stayed overnight in Shenzhen, up a staggering 70% compared with a year earlier, according to city government data. In 2026, more than 6.6 million foreign tourists visited the city, mostly from countries in the Asia-Pacific region. And these figures don’t account for the more than 10 million visitors in 2025 from the nearby semi-autonomous Chinese cities of Hong Kong and Macao – a 25% jump on 2024. Shenzhen has become a popular destination for Hong Kongers to spend the weekend, thanks to its proximity (just a 14-minute high-speed rail journey) and its relative affordability. Unsurprisingly, the first thing Western visitors notice about Shenzhen is its tech-forward vibe. Megan Jarrett, a South Carolina native in her early thirties who called Shenzhen home for three years from 2023, told CNN she loved living there. “It is high-tech and modern, it is very convenient, but to me, it was also very friendly,” she said. Will McCaskill, a 28-year-old video producer based in London, visited in May. “Everything that could be a screen was a screen or a drone or whatever. [Shenzhen] was very forward in that regard,” he said. But what surprised him was that the city didn’t feel busy, or intense. “You’ll drive past this really dense, built-up area with lots of skyscrapers, but then on the street level, it’s quite calm or just quite local.” “The city is so clean, well-built and easy to navigate.” Chen, the university professor, said she is proud to be a Shenzhen native – a rare distinction in a city constantly attracting outsiders to live, work and settle. Official data shows about half a million people move to Shenzhen from elsewhere in China each year. “Because Shenzhen is such a young city, you get this sense that everything is changing at an incredible pace. The metro system is still expanding nonstop, and the high-speed rail network is constantly being upgraded to run faster,” said Chen. “You just feel that things are always moving forward here.” Going, doing, and seeing China has made it easier than ever to visit in the past few years. UK and EU nationals enjoy visa-free entry to China. American tourists do too – sort of. Travelers can fly into Shenzhen and stay within Guangdong province – which also includes the megacity of Guangzhou – for up to 10 days, but must fly out to a third destination outside mainland China. That can include Hong Kong and Macao. Shenzhen is also easy to visit from neighboring Hong Kong, which has six border-crossing points with Shenzhen (a passport is required, as Hong Kong is a Special Administrative Region of China). The easiest option is simply to take the subway, as the city’s East Rail Line goes from Admiralty Station in central Hong Kong to either Lo Wu or Lok Ma Chau at the border. There are also buses, the bullet train and even ferry options. Meanwhile, Shenzhen’s Bao’an Airport is constantly adding new routes for air travelers. These days, it has nonstop flights to Los Angeles as well as more and more destinations in the Asia-Pacific region like Kuala Lumpur, Melbourne and Surabaya in Indonesia. Many expats have settled in Shekou district in the city’s southeast. These days, it has a chilled-out vibe with bars and restaurants serving up global cuisines. Huaqiangbei – the world’s largest electronics market – is worth a stop. More than 100,000 businesses pack into the building’s dense, maze-like grids and sell their goods at cheap prices. But Shenzhen is working hard to become known for more than just low-cost food and electronics. The city has a growing number of new museums. The Stockholm-founded museum Fotografiska just opened a Shenzhen outpost in October. In May, the city celebrated the opening of Shenzhen International Museum of Art, which houses works from Renaissance painters Titian and Tintoretto, seven Chinese zodiac bronze animal heads, renowned Chinese calligraphy and pieces from art masters Qi Baishi and Zhang Daqian. CNN’s Sierra Chen contributed to reporting.

articles.summary: Iran-aligned Kataib Hezbollah says the group is subjected to ‘blackmail’ to force disarmament amid US pressure on Iraq.
articles.body:
The Iran-aligned Kataib Hezbollah group has denied its involvement in an oil smuggling operation in Iraq’s Jurf al-Nasr area after Iraqi authorities launched an anticorruption crackdown.

Kataib Hezbollah, one of Iraq’s most heavily armed factions, said in a statement on Sunday that the Iraqi prime minister’s office was “fabricating lies” and that the group was being subjected to “the largest blackmail operation” to force its disarmament .

The statement was issued a day after Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi sacked nine senior officials following an investigation into the allegations.

The Iraqi government said an investigation committee, chaired by al-Zaidi, confirmed oil smuggling based on “intelligence documents” containing satellite images showing operations being carried out in the armed faction’s stronghold.

The committee ordered those implicated, whom it did not identify, to be referred to the judiciary and dismissed nine officials, including security and intelligence officers in Babil province, an Interior Ministry commander and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company at the Ministry of Oil.

Responding to the committee’s findings, Kataib Hezbollah said the investigation “found no violations whatsoever of the oil pipelines” and that this “definitively proves that the smuggling allegations are false”.

The group said its members accompanied the committee’s visit to the Jurf al-Nasr area on Friday.

Baghdad has been under increasing pressure from Washington to rein in Iran-aligned groups and curb Tehran’s influence in Iraq, an ally of both the US and Iran.

Al-Zaidi has previously promised to ensure that non-state armed groups would hand over their weapons to the state.

However, Kataib Hezbollah has pledged to retain its weapons arsenal and accused al-Zaidi of caving to pressure from the US, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

Iran-aligned groups, including Kataib Hezbollah, have previously targeted US forces in Iraq and attacked Gulf states following the start of the US-Israel war on Iran in late February.

Washington accuses Tehran of using Iraq’s economy to evade sanctions and has previously sanctioned Iraqi individuals for blending Iraqi and Iranian oil.

articles.title: Lincolnshire Wildlife Trust secures cash for Hawthorpe reserve
articles.summary: Lincolnshire Wildlife Trust reaches its funding target to buy grassland habitat near Hawthorpe.
articles.body:
A wildlife trust has raised money to buy a large grassland habitat and turn it into a nature reserve.

Lincolnshire Wildlife Trust said public donations worth £400,000 meant it was able to secure 215 acres (87 hectares) of land near Hawthorpe.

The trust was previously awarded a £1m grant from Biffa Award, as part of the Landfill Communities Fund, towards the purchase.

Paul Learoyd, chief executive of the trust, said: "It is thanks to people's generosity that the long-term protection of the grassland has been secured."

He described the site as a "hidden gem" and "quite unique" for Lincolnshire, as it had not been actively farmed for more than 40 years.

The grassland supports a wide range of species, including ground-nesting birds such as skylark and linnet, according to surveys.

The trust said it was completing paperwork for the purchase but had an agreement in place to safeguard the site, which could now be turned into a thriving reserve for wildlife, wildflowers and wetland species.

An appeal to raise the £1.4m needed to buy the land, between Grantham and Bourne, was launched a year ago.

Learoyd explained: "The land came up for sale on the open market which meant that the funds for the purchase had to be secured relatively urgently.

"We have been overwhelmed by the response.

"There is still paperwork to process but, once complete, Hawthorpe will become the trust's newest nature reserve."

Rachel Maidment, grants manager at Biffa, previously said the scheme would deliver "huge benefits" for nature, climate resilience and local communities.

In September, the trust learnt of plans to build a pipeline through Hawthorpe as part of a proposed new reservoir on land south of Sleaford.

The trust has said it had "opened a dialogue" with Anglian Water over the plans, which are undergoing a third public consultation, and would submit a formal objection over the route of the pipeline.

"We are deeply concerned about the potential impact of the pipeline and its construction on this valuable grassland habitat and the wildlife that depends on it," the trust said in October.

Anglian Water has been contacted for comment. It previously said the reservoir was a key part of its plans to "secure water supplies to Lincolnshire and the wider region for generations to come" and pointed to "the driest March to September period in the East of England since records began in 1899".
